name: recursive-descent-parser
intent: Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step.
problem: A hand-written parser is the only option - no generator in the toolchain, or the grammar is a small DSL - yet the grammar is not a flat token sequence: alternatives must be chosen from lookahead, repetition must become a loop, and the natural grammar for expressions is left-recursive, which a top-down parser cannot translate directly. Without a disciplined mapping from rules to functions the parser degenerates into ad-hoc index arithmetic and exception-driven backtracking, and errors end up without positions.
context: Front ends for small languages, DSLs, query/filter/rule grammars, configuration and protocol formats, and the parsing layer of compilers and interpreters that want no code-generation step. It applies when a lexer or token stream already exists (or is cheap to write), the grammar is small to medium and reasonably LL-friendly or rewritable into LL form, and the team values readable, step-debuggable, position-precise parsing over generated tables.
benefits: The grammar is executable and readable: one named function per rule, with alternatives as branches, repetition as loops and rule references as calls, so the code can be reviewed rule by rule against the grammar.

No toolchain step and no generated artifacts: the parser is ordinary source code that builds, debugs, profiles and versions with the rest of the program; there is no grammar file, generator version or build plugin to keep in sync.

Diagnostics are first-class: because the parser knows which token it expected at which position, errors can carry exact positions, expected sets, notes and recovery behaviour - the quality bar IDE, linter and compiler tooling actually needs.
Cheap to start and cheap to extend: adding a rule or an alternative is a function or a branch, there is no regeneration step, and small grammars stay reviewable in a single file.

Fits lexing strategies that generators handle badly: scannerless parsing, indentation-sensitive layout, context-dependent tokenization and custom token streams can be handled exactly where the grammar needs it.

Testable rule by rule: each rule function can be called at a chosen position with a prepared token fixture, so parser behaviour is unit-testable and failures reproduce without a generator's indirection.
tradeoffs: Recursion depth grows with input nesting and most runtimes do not eliminate tail calls, so deeply nested or adversarial input exhausts the call stack; the parser needs an explicit depth guard, which the pattern itself does not provide.

Left recursion is unsupported and must be rewritten into loops (A = A b | c becomes A = c b*), which is exactly where the code and the grammar diverge and where precedence and associativity bugs hide.

The code is the grammar: there is no declarative artifact to diff, validate or hand to a tool, so grammar changes are code changes spread over several functions and review cost grows with grammar size.
Error recovery and messages are hand-crafted per rule; the pattern offers no structure for diagnostics, whereas generated parsers ship expected-set reporting and recovery for free.

Backtracking without memoization can be exponential in the input size, and memoizing it costs memory proportional to the input (the sibling memoizing-parser pattern) - predictability holds only while the grammar stays predictive.

Larger or fast-moving grammars turn into maintenance: one function per rule plus precedence strata duplicate lookahead and consumption patterns, and a generator or toolkit becomes cheaper well before the grammar reaches programming-language size.

It presupposes LL discipline: ambiguity, common prefixes and long lookahead must be engineered away (factoring, precedence climbing, predicates), so the grammar can end up shaped by the parser rather than by the language.

participants.responsibility: One per grammar production: consumes the tokens its rule matches, calls the functions of referenced rules, and returns the parsed node, value or error.
Supplies typed tokens with source positions - a separate lexer, a scanner object or a scannerless character-level reader; rule bodies never inspect raw characters.
Shared peek/at/match/expect primitives that own index arithmetic and produce positioned errors, so rule bodies read like grammar productions.
The mutable per-parse state (position, lookahead, recursion depth, diagnostics sink, scope state) owned by one parser instance and never shared between parses.
Constructs the nodes, values or instructions for matched constructs; in single-pass compilers it emits code directly instead of building a tree.
Turns a mismatch into a positioned diagnostic with the expected set and decides whether to abort, synchronise at a rule boundary, or insert a missing token and continue.

use_cases: Front ends for small languages, DSLs and configuration formats (filter expressions, rule engines, policy languages, template syntaxes) where a generator and its build integration would be overkill.
Expression and statement parsing in single-pass compilers and interpreters that emit bytecode or IR while parsing, as in Crafting Interpreters' Lox.
Tooling for a grammar you own - formatters, linters, syntax highlighters, language servers - where error tolerance, multiple diagnostics and exact positions matter more than raw throughput.
Protocol and wire-format decoding with a small fixed grammar, where errors must carry byte offsets and malformed input must be rejected deterministically.
Context-dependent or indentation-sensitive syntaxes (templates with interpolation, layout-based blocks, configuration with embedded expressions) that a generated lexer handles poorly.
Codebases that must not carry generated code: security-reviewed, vendored or cross-compiled projects where an ordinary source file beats a build-time generator.
Clang's C-family front end uses a unified hand-built recursive-descent parser for C, C++, Objective-C and Objective-C++, pairing rule-oriented control flow with production-quality diagnostics.
The Go standard library's go/parser is a production recursive-descent parser for Go source, with explicit parser state, nesting-depth guards and error recovery.
rustc_parse is the Rust compiler's recursive-descent parser module, showing how a hand-written parser can scale to macros, recovery modes and detailed token/state handling.

Lua's reference implementation compiles with lparser.c, a single-pass recursive-descent parser that emits bytecode opcodes while reducing expressions instead of building a syntax tree, with precedence handled by parsing levels.
avoid_when: The grammar is large, ambiguous or changes frequently: a parser generator or parser toolkit (bison/yacc, ANTLR, lark, a PEG toolkit) keeps the grammar declarative and maintains the tables, lookahead and recovery for you.

The language's own parser already exists and can be reused (go/parser, Roslyn's Syntax API, the TypeScript compiler API, Python's ast/compile): writing a second parser for the same syntax is duplicated work.
The grammar is naturally left-recursive and cannot be rewritten cleanly: LR/GLR generators or a packrat/PEG engine with left-recursion support handle it directly.
Only a fixed data format needs reading (JSON, CSV, XML, protobuf): a standard-library or schema-driven reader is simpler, faster and better tested.
The parser must be incremental or error-tolerant for an editor: a framework designed for that (Roslyn, tree-sitter, SwiftParser-style designs) beats a hand-rolled parser.
The grammar is a flat token sequence with no nesting: a loop over tokens or a regular-expression pass is enough.
anti_patterns: Translating a left-recursive rule literally and "fixing" the infinite recursion with a depth counter or by catching the stack overflow, instead of rewriting the rule into a loop.
Duplicating lookahead and consumption logic inside every rule instead of shared peek/expect helpers, so error positions and messages drift apart.
A hand-written parser for a grammar that changes every sprint, leaving the grammar only in code and every change spread over several rule functions.
Parsing untrusted input with unbounded recursion and accepting stack exhaustion as the failure mode.
Keeping the expression grammar as a ladder of near-identical functions per precedence level when precedence climbing or a Pratt parser would collapse it into one loop.
Silent recovery - skipping tokens until something parses - so malformed input produces a plausible tree instead of a diagnostic.
Ignoring the lexer: raw string operations and character indexing inside rule functions, which turns the parser into an unmaintainable scanner-parser tangle.
design_principles: One rule, one function: the call graph mirrors the grammar, so the code is the specification and the specification is readable.
Explicit lookahead: alternatives are chosen by inspected tokens; speculative parsing and exception-driven backtracking are deliberate design decisions, not accidents.
Separate lexing from parsing unless scannerless parsing is deliberate: tokens carry kinds and positions, and rule bodies never touch characters.
Design the error path together with the grammar: positioned errors, expected sets and a recovery strategy per rule boundary.
Keep the grammar LL-friendly: factor common prefixes, eliminate left recursion mechanically, and move precedence into loops or precedence climbing.
Single responsibility per rule and no cross-rule state beyond the cursor: shared mutable state makes recursion order observable and tests order-dependent.
best_practices: Write the grammar down (EBNF or a commented rule table) next to the rule functions and change both in the same commit.
Centralise token consumption in a small set of helpers (peek/at/match/expect) that produce positioned errors with the expected token set.
Rewrite left recursion mechanically (A = A b | c becomes A = c (b)*) and let the loop build the left-associative tree.
Stratify expression precedence or use precedence climbing, and switch to a Pratt parser when the operator set is large or user-extensible.
Guard recursion depth and token count explicitly before parsing untrusted input, failing with a positioned error before the host stack limit is reached.
Choose a recovery strategy deliberately - synchronise on statement boundaries, insert missing tokens, or stop at the first error - and test it with malformed fixtures.
Test rule functions individually with token fixtures, plus end-to-end tests that assert error positions; keep the parser free of I/O so both stay trivial.
Keep the parser one-pass and side-effect free until the AST is built: do not resolve symbols or types inside rules (that is a later pass).
sources: Nystrom, R., Crafting Interpreters (2021), §6.2 Recursive Descent Parsing - a recursive descent parser is a literal translation of the grammar's rules into imperative code: each rule becomes a function, terminals consume tokens, alternatives become if/switch, repetition becomes a loop, optionals become conditionals; left recursion must be eliminated by rewriting the rule, and GCC, V8 and Roslyn are named as production users.

Parr, T., Language Implementation Patterns (Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2010), ch. 2 with patterns 1-4: Mapping Grammars to Recursive-Descent Recognizers, LL(1) Recursive-Descent Lexer, LL(1) Recursive-Descent Parser, LL(k) Recursive-Descent Parser.

Aho, A. V., Sethi, R. & Ullman, J. D., Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools (Addison-Wesley, 1986) - the top-down parsing chapter (§4.4, Recursive-Descent Parsing): predictive parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW sets and left-recursion elimination.
Conway, M. E. (1963). Design of a separable transition-diagram compiler. Communications of the ACM 6(7), 396-408 - the COBOL compiler usually credited as the first recursive-descent implementation.
